HEADLINE: Faster loans as NAB rides cloud investing wave
TEXT:
National Australia Bank's venture capital fund has led a $US24 million ($32 million) equity capital raising by the Canadian cloud computing firm Wave, in a deal that illustrates a realisation by banks that access to data will improve risk assessment.

It also highlights awareness by software developers that adding financial services capability could boost growth.

NAB Ventures said it could not disclose the dollar amount of the investment, the fund's fourth after taking non-controlling minority stakes in start-ups Veem, Medipass and Data Republic.

NAB joins Royal Bank of Canada as a new Wave shareholder, after the series D round was backed by existing owners including Omers Ventures, the VC arm of the Ontario pension fund. NAB will appoint an observer to the Wave board.

Wave is planning on using RBC and NAB to integrate financial services into the software, which is free for users. It makes revenue from fees relating to invoice, payments and payroll services, and is experimenting with lending products.

Banking executives consider the arrival of cloud-based accounting as a potentially disruptive force for business banking, given live data captured in financial statements is typically better quality than information held by banks and can be used to price credit and assess risk, which are core banking functions.

NAB Ventures general partner Melissa Widner said it was too early to say how the relationship with Wave would unfold, but she suggested the deal might help NAB make faster loan approvals in the future. NAB's QuickBiz business loan product is already integrated with cloud accounting providers Xero and MYOB to accelerate approval times.

Ms Widner points to a future where small businesses might be able to get instant funding as the data stored in the accounting cloud gives a bank a real-time picture of risk.

"Looking at data in general, instead of doing a loan application like you do today, what if you could push a button and have funds directly in your account? That is, in the long term, how lending will happen."

Wave co-founder and CEO Kirk Simpson said surveys showed the average small business owner took 33 hours to prepare for a loan application.

NAB's technology makes things faster than this global number, but "at the end of day, it takes way too long to walk into a bank and get a loan," Mr Simpson said.

"The majority of business borrowers are not pre-approved, because data is hard to obtain and it's hard to get a sense of whether this is a good customer or not. By looking at accounting, invoicing and tax compliance data, you can make that decision much easier."

Wave, founded seven years ago with 120 employees, has Australian customers in the tens of thousands without having done any marketing. Globally, it has more than 2 million small business customers in more than 200 countries.

The cloud accounting market is crowded, with Intuit and Sage the other major players, but Wave reckons its system is the only one that has been built to appeal specifically to sole proprietors, or businesses with fewer than 10 employees and less than $2 million in revenue. These businesses typically keep their financial information in shoe boxes or messy spreadsheets and find alternative cloud offerings too complex.

In the US and Canada, Wave conducts payroll processing and tax filings, and has begun trials in lending via a partnership with NYSE-listed OnDeck, which is also working with Commonwealth Bank of Australia.

It also makes money on processing credit card transactions.

HEADLINE: Jobs fear as energy debate flares
TEXT:
The Turnbull government has moved to pre-empt the findings of its Chief Scientist on energy market reform by ruling out an emissions intensity scheme and giving the green light to the Clean Energy Finance Corporation to invest in carbon capture and storage coal technology.

The controversial moves came as a threat by Glencore to cease copper processing in Queensland, mainly due to the volatility and cost of energy, was echoed by other manufacturers who said more refineries and smelters would close unless energy price and security was resolved. Manufacturers including BASF warned there was limited chance of new investment in Australia and further job cuts were likely.

Alumina Ltd chairman John Pizzey said company boards across the nation were now making decisions based on energy security.

"The cost of energy is becoming an investment decision criteria, more and more people will be making Glencore-type decisions," he said.

Tomago chief executive Matt Howell, who runs Australia's largest aluminium smelter in the NSW Hunter region, said the company was considering cutting production due to "ridiculously high" wholesale electricity prices, which would result in job losses.

The Glencore ultimatum - in which it will not guarantee its Mount Isa copper smelter and its Townsville copper refinery beyond 12 months - has injected urgency into the political debate, but there was no sign of the bipartisan policy approach that business says is desperately needed to provide investor certainty.

Business, industry, federal Labor and the energy market regulators are advocating an emissions intensity scheme to bring down emissions over time while creating long-term certainty for investors to provide new forms of energy. An EIS is also likely to be a key recommendation of Chief Scientist Alan Finkel when his final report on energy market policy is handed to the Prime Minister and premiers on Friday next week.

But Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull told his party room on Tuesday there would neither be an emissions trading scheme nor an EIS.

Mr Turnbull said the public was looking for leadership on energy with many households under pressure from rising prices.

The federal government blamed state Labor's 50 per cent renewable energy target plus price gouging by local coal-fired power generators for the Glencore threat. Federal Labor said it underscored the need for the Turnbull government to adopt an EIS.

"Industry as well as experts are crying out for an emissions intensity scheme for the electricity sector, to end uncertainty and fuel new investment, but Turnbull and [Resources Minister Josh] Frydenberg have made it clear they will continue to put the interests of the hard right of their party above what is best for the country," shadow energy minister Mark Butler said.

"This isn't good enough. Not just Glencore, but thousands of other jobs and whole industries are at stake."

At the same time the government ruled out an EIS, it enshrined its belief in coal as an ongoing source of power generation by introducing legislation to enable the Clean Energy Finance Corporation to invest in carbon capture and storage.

The CEFC is a $10 billion taxpayer-funded loan facility established by Labor to invest in the development of renewable and other clean energy sources.

Months after first flagging the move, Mr Frydenberg announced the government will legislate to expand the CEFC's mandate so it can invest in carbon capture and storage technology which, if ever successfully developed, will enable emissions from coal-fired power stations to be kept out of the atmosphere. The CEFC will not be investing in other so-called clean coal technology such as the construction of a High Efficiency Low Emissions (HELE) power station.

Mr Frydenberg said coal had a future, more so if emissions could be reduced using CCS technology that, he claimed, was "a proven technology with 22 large-scale projects either in operation or under construction overseas".

"Given that CCS technology has received such strong support from the likes of the International Panel on Climate Change and the International Energy Agency internationally as well as the Chief Scientist and the CSIRO here at home, it is now only appropriate that we unshackle the CEFC and allow it to support this low-emissions technology," he said.

The move was welcomed by the Business Council of Australia as well as miners BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto but condemned by the Greens and environmental groups. Labor made no comment.

"No option should be excluded from the search for solutions to Australia's energy challenges," said Joanne Farrell, managing director of Rio Tinto Australia

HEADLINE: Signs of property market cooling
TEXT:
The number of new interest-only loans to home buyers across the nation dropped in the March quarter in a sign that a crackdown on speculative property investment may be working.

Only 1685 new interest-only loans were made by banks in the period, according to the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, down slightly from 1692 previously. APRA considers interest-only loans to be risky.

Treasurer Scott Morrison tweeted that the number of interest-only loans had fallen for the first time since 2009 and that in dollar terms the share of the loans was 10 percentage points below the peak level two years ago.

APRA's data was followed by further evidence that the nation's two largest housing markets were cooling, with Sydney residential property values down 1.3 per cent and Melbourne falling 1.8 per cent in May, according to CoreLogic.

A full breakdown of the monthly figures to be released tomorrow will show a 1.1 per cent decline across the five largest capital cities.

The housing construction boom also continued to slow in April, with the number of new apartment approvals falling to the lowest level in two years. As projects under way are completed and not replaced, the slowdown is likely to accelerate.

HEADLINE: Scandal ridden
TEXT: Tax Commissioner Chris Jordan knew for months police were closing in on the family of deputy tax commissioner Michael Cranston, who had made a "huge error of judgment" trying to access records on behalf of his son. Mr Jordan conceded the allegations over the Plutus Payroll tax fraud ring had "struck at the heart and values" of the ATO.

HEADLINE: Morrison slams bank 'oligopoly'
TEXT:
Treasurer Scott Morrison has attacked the banking sector oligopoly, accusing it of using its pricing power to the detriment of all Australians as it was revealed the first payment for the bank levy would be delayed by three months.

In a speech that was highly critical of the big four banks, the Treasurer said the levy was introduced to support competition in the banking sector.

He zeroed in on the cheaper cost of funding, benefits flowing from the internal based modelling and dominant market share as advantages enjoyed by the big four that bolstered their positions against would-be competitors.

He said concentration of market power in banking had contributed to "systemic risk" and that the government was not prepared to sit back and watch the imbalances further entrench the position of the banks.

"The House of Representatives Economics Committee's 'Review of the Four Major Banks', commissioned by the government last year, concluded that Australia's banking sector is an oligopoly and that Australia's largest banks have significant pricing power which they have used to the detriment of everyday Australians. This is not a situation that the government is willing to accept," Mr Morrison said.

The speech coincided with the release of the draft legislation for the Major Bank Levy, which revealed that the first payment would not fall due until March 21, two new exclusions and estimated compliance costs for the banks of $15 million.

Mr Morrison said pushing the first payment back was not expected to come at a revenue cost, with the draft legislation explaining the government was expecting payments for the September and December quarters on March 21.

He also took the opportunity to warn the banks not to pass on the costs to customers and said they needed to "balance the needs of borrowers, savers, shareholders and the wider community".

The Australian Bankers' Association chief executive, Anna Bligh, seized on the adjustments as a major backdown on what she described as a rushed and hastily designed policy.

"Banks welcome the concessions which would have had unintended consequences across the financial system, but despite these changes, major banks remain concerned about the government's poorly designed tax grab," she said.

Among the new detail released about the tax was the decision to exclude Exchange Settlement Balances (ESBs) held with the Reserve Bank and derivatives used by the banks to offset risk.

Data from the Reserve Bank of Australia shows that there was about $27.4 billion in ESBs system wide as of Wednesday, May 24.

Shares in the big four banks and Macquarie Group rallied on Tuesday in line with the market, with ANZ up 0.8 per cent, Commonwealth Bank up 0.7 per cent, National Australia Bank up 1.7 per cent, Macquarie up 0.8 per cent and Westpac up 1 per cent.

The ABA said the bank levy would be a tax on all Australians without an end until it included a sunset clause, and that every Australian with a bank account, a home loan or a superannuation account would be affected by the levy.

Ms Bligh rounded on the government's consultation process with the industry that amounted to a single hour-long meeting with Treasury officials two days after the policy was announced on budget night.

Ms Bligh also said that while the ABA would not launch a co-ordinated advertising campaign similar to the anti-mining tax movement, the banks targeted would continue to push the government to widen the net by including foreign banks.

This was confirmed by senior banking sources who said that although they were pleased that the rate of levy would be enshrined by law that the levy should be expanded to foreign banks and should have an end date.

Satisfaction with the capping of the 6 basis point levy may be shortlived however, with The Tax Institute saying the draft legislation amounted to law by ministerial decree.

Senior tax counsel Professor Robert Deutsch said the wording of the legislation left it open for the relevant minister to interpret the specifics of how a bank's total liabilities would be calculated.

"There is something distinctly uncomfortable about a law that says - generally this is how you work it out but the Minister can tell you what the precise rules are as we go and can even changes the rules as he or she has previously applied them," Professor Deutsch said.

The draft however revealed that government had consulted more widely than had initially been speculated, including that it sounded out the banks on changes to expand the regulators powers over the remuneration of bank executives. It also stated that Treasury had engaged in discussions about data needed to enact the bank levy.

HEADLINE: Big Four get pitching for massive bank contract
TEXT:
Australia's big four banks are preparing to battle for one of the market's biggest banking contracts.

Street Talk understands Victoria's Department of Treasury and Finance wrote to the banks last week, pointing out that its existing $50 million-plus-a-year contract with Westpac Banking Corp would expire next year and seeking ideas for the next agreement.

The way Victoria sees it, a lot has changed in financial services since its last deal with Westpac in 2011. There have been advances in technology, banking products, infrastructure, ledger systems and the like, and it wants to get the best deal next time around.

So the state sent a list of 67 questions to the banks, fintechs and other interested parties, asking for their ideas on what the new contract should consider by early July. It wanted to know about things like streamlined payment systems, data analytics, block chain technology and virtual credit cards.

Victoria told the banks it would put the contract for its core transactional banking, customer payment services and purchase cards to the market next year.

The existing seven-year contract - worth more than $200 million when signed as a five-year deal with Westpac in 2011 - expires in September 2018.

It'll be interesting to see whether Commonwealth Bank, ANZ or NAB - or a bolter - can knock off the incumbent.

Governments are traditionally conservative when it comes to their core banking infrastructure and contracts tend to be sticky.

Victoria's proposed contract comes only six months after Westpac won an extension on a similar transactions and card services deal it has with NSW.

HEADLINE: Westpac clamps down
TEXT:
Westpac Banking Corp's mortgage broking team has written to clients to outline some material changes to interest only lending.

Street Talk understands that Westpac brokers told clients on Tuesday that the bank would curb lending for new and existing interest only borrowers, reducing the maximum loan to value ratio to 80 per cent.

The bank said that rule applied for both new loans and loan increases as of Monday, June 5.

It said the only exceptions were for building and construction loans where interest only would be available during the construction period before switching to principal and interest repayments, for up to 12-months of parental leave, and bridging loans.

Westpac also said it would waive fees for clients switching from interest only repayments to principal plus interest repayments.

The bank said the policy changes were aimed at meeting regulatory requirements.

"These changes will help us continue to meet our regulatory requirements and apply responsible lending practices in assessing a customer's ability to service existing and proposed debts," Westpac's brokers told clients.

HEADLINE: Cromwell's Weightman lures Starwood Capital as backer
TEXT:
For Cromwell's managing director Paul Weightman - whose long-running pursuit of Investa Office Fund has earned him the moniker "Waity, Waity" - it may be a case of better late than never.

Weightman's ambitious plan to buy out IOF for around $3 billion has been bedevilled by a lack of unidentified funders, creating considerable uncertainty over whether the money is really there to do the deal.

Now it seems that US private equity giant Starwood Capital is at least showing some interest in the proposed takeover plan.

Starwood sent a team out to Brisbane to look at a number of assets last week and also went to Sydney as the private equiteer mulls whether to commit to Weightman's vision.

Weightman's ambition appeared to take a near-fatal hit this month with the candid admission from South Africa's Redefine Properties, Cromwell's biggest shareholder, that it would not back the deal with its own funds.

Even with a group of banks in his corner, Weightman would still have to stump up an equity cheque of at least $1.5 billion.

Weightman has already been booted out of the IOF data room by the directors, who have had enough and just want Cromwell to put up or move on.

As Weightman ponders that dilemma, he has won a very short reprieve, with IOF investors preparing to vote on a proposal for IOF to buy part control of its management platform. Major proxy advisers don't like it and the investors may vote it down.

Elsewhere, and as first reported by Street Talk, Credit Suisse capital markets banker Adam Lennen has been charged with leading the firm's Melbourne-based investment banking team.

It's understood Credit Suisse told staff last week that Lennen would take the role as head of investment banking and capital markets for the Melbourne office, in addition to his job as co-head of equity capital markets for Australia.

Lennen is a long-serving Credit Suisse banker who joined the Swiss bank in 2000 and has since specialised in ECM deals.

It comes amid a busier than usual flurry of senior investment banker movements and promotions across the industry in recent months.

Most recently, Morgan Stanley appointed Bryce Thompson and Bob Herbert as head of equity capital markets and head of fixed income capital markets respectively, while Goldman Sachs poached a new pair of equities co-heads from Macquarie last week.

HEADLINE: Offshore lender flicks the switch on CHAMP's Gerard
TEXT:
Is this the blown globe that cuts financial power to the ailing Gerard Lighting?

Street Talk can reveal one of the lenders to Australasia's largest lighting distribution and partnership network is set to sell its loan.

While it should be noted that there's nothing official yet - and it's a sensitive time in the business - sources pointed to the leveraged finance arm of industrials giant Siemens as the seller.

Siemens is believed to have about a $20 million to $30 million exposure to Gerard, and Bain Capital Credit, the rebadged Sankaty Advisors, is tipped as the buyer.

Bain Capital Credit knows the company well. It picked up a stake in Gerard's debt stack when it bought GE Capital's Australian and New Zealand commercial finance business in 2015.

If the trade is successful, it's understood Bain Capital Credit is supportive of turning the business around and injecting new money into it.

It's the latest development at Gerard, and comes as the company and its private equity owner, CHAMP, have been in regular meetings with the lending group, led by Westpac. The bank is known to have had Gerard on its "troubled" list for some time.

Gerard is behind well-known lighting brands such as Pierlite, Sylvania, Crompton and Moonlighting. The business operates in a fiercely competitive industry subject to intense pricing pressures as imported products jostle for extra sales. CHAMP made a $186 million takeover in 2012 which in hindsight wasn't one of their best moves.

The Gerard family originally floated the business on the ASX in mid-2010 but still had around half of it after the IPO.

As first reported by this column in May 2016, UBS had been working with CHAMP on strategies for Gerard which could include the sale of a unit, a partnership with an offshore group or a broader deal involving the company in its entirety. However, the process was put on ice earlier this year.

HEADLINE: Month end sharpens broker rivalries
TEXT:
It's that time of the month again!

Equities desks go toe-to-toe today seeking to capitalise on fund managers' month-end trading and pick up share on what is traditionally one of the busiest trading days of the month.

This time around, there are some bruised brokers who have been treading carefully around their beaten up clients.

The market is off about 3.5 per cent for the month, led by the Big Four banks who have been sold heavily since budget day three weeks ago, and it has been hard work finding winners.

Equities desk heads reckon offshore investors are retreating, while corporate activity is patchy and there are big questions about the initial public offering window which has kept plenty of bankers and brokers in jobs over the past four years.

It has been just as hard in small caps thanks to a plethora of company profit downgrades. And now plenty of fundies are worried about their likely performance numbers for the year to June 30 and what it will mean for annual bonus payments.

Perhaps it would be better for them to have another bad month in June and start from a low base next financial year.

Among the brokers, UBS is set to finish May well out in front in terms of cash equities market share, while the main battle is between Deutsche Bank and Morgan Stanley for second place.

Citi and Bank of America Merrill Lynch round out the top five for the month to date, according to IRESS, ahead of JPMorgan, Macquarie's institutional business, Credit Suisse and Goldman Sachs.

The calendar year-to-date numbers are much the same, particularly at the top of the table.

MYOB is also expected to remain a keen talking point today.

While brokers did their best to shake free Bain's 39 per cent worth about $800 million earlier this week, the private equity firm was unwilling to budge.

It's understood Bain received a bid for the whole stake at $3.25 a share on Monday night, and bids for smaller portions at higher levels. Only last week, Goldman Sachs tried to take a $200 million piece at $3.40 a share.

Brokers are expected to go back to the private equity investor in coming days, with the stock now free of a voluntary escrow.

Bain last reduced its stake at $3.55 a share in February.
